Choosing an insurance deductible: compare the premium and the cash you retain

Explore four graphics that separate recurring premiums, per-claim responsibility and the reserve needed for a covered loss.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore premiums, deductibles and cash reserves

Interactive planning lab

Annual household cost · A$1,700
Annual household cost · B$2,400
One-claim reserve gap · B$500

Hypothetical policies with identical otherwise-unlimited coverage for the entered eligible loss. Deductible applies separately to each claim; the household pays the smaller of covered loss and deductible. Annual cost metrics use the selected claim count and include premiums plus retained losses. No exclusions, policy limits, co-insurance, annual deductible aggregation, premium changes after claims, settlement delay or claim probabilities are modeled. Premiums and deductibles are assumptions, not quotations or coverage recommendations.

On this page

  1. Identify the recurring price and the contingent amount
  2. Read how the deductible interacts with loss size

The central idea

A premium reduction and a larger per-claim cash commitment belong in the same comparison. Check whether the household can fund the retained risk when a loss occurs.

01

Identify the recurring price and the contingent amount

A premium is paid to maintain the insurance arrangement. A deductible determines part of the loss the household retains when the relevant claim conditions apply. The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada’s insurance overview explains these terms and notes that a higher deductible may be associated with a lower premium.

The comparison uses two hypothetical policies with otherwise identical coverage for the eligible loss. Policy A defaults to a CAD 1,200 annual premium and CAD 500 per-claim deductible. Policy B defaults to CAD 900 and CAD 1,500 respectively. These inputs are not quotations or terms from an insurer.

The annual premium saving in B is CAD 300. That recurring saving comes with an additional retained amount for some claims. The controls let either policy have the higher premium or deductible, so read the signs and the actual figures rather than assuming the labels A and B imply a ranking.

02

Read how the deductible interacts with loss size

The first chart shows household responsibility against the size of a fully eligible loss. In this simplified model, household share = minimum of covered loss and deductible. The assumed insurer share is the remaining eligible loss, with no limit or other cost sharing applied.

If a covered loss is CAD 300 and the deductible is CAD 500, the household pays CAD 300, not CAD 500. Once the eligible loss exceeds the deductible, the retained amount stops increasing in this model. The curve therefore rises, then flattens at the selected deductible.

This chart isolates deductible arithmetic. Real exclusions, sublimits, valuation methods, policy limits and settlement conditions can change the amount covered. Some policies also use other deductible structures. Verify those terms before treating two premium-and-deductible pairs as equivalent coverage.

03

Compare several realized claim years

The grouped bars add annual premiums to the retained amount for zero, one, two or three covered claims. Each claim has the loss amount entered in the controls, and a new deductible applies separately to each claim. The selected claim count is also a scenario input, without a probability attached.

For the default CAD 5,000 eligible loss, one claim costs the household CAD 1,700 under A and CAD 2,400 under B, including the annual premium. With no claims, the comparison is simply CAD 1,200 versus CAD 900. The order can change because the recurring and contingent amounts respond differently.

The model does not calculate an expected annual cost, predict claim frequency or apply a premium increase after a claim. A year with no claims does not show that coverage had no value, and a lower modeled cost in one scenario does not establish which policy is suitable.

04

Check the retained amount against accessible cash

The split bars show how the selected eligible loss is allocated between household and insurer under the assumptions. With a CAD 5,000 loss, B leaves CAD 1,500 with the household and CAD 3,500 with the insurer. Premiums are excluded from this per-claim split because they are already counted in the annual comparison.

The default CAD 1,000 of cash allocated to a claim leaves a CAD 500 one-claim reserve gap under B. That gap is separate from the premium budget. If more than one claim occurs, or another emergency uses the reserve first, additional cash may be needed.

Settlement timing can also matter. The retained share does not necessarily equal all the cash required before reimbursement arrives. The tool does not model repair deposits, temporary accommodation, claim delays or access restrictions on savings. Keep money already assigned to another goal out of the available-claim reserve unless replacement funding is planned.

05

Read the matrix as a stress comparison

The matrix varies claim size and count, showing B’s annual household cost minus A’s. A negative cell means B costs less within that scenario; a positive cell means B costs more. It uses the entered premiums and deductibles while replacing the selected claim size and count with the displayed alternatives.

Use the matrix to locate the circumstances that change the result. Then consider whether the corresponding retained costs could be paid on time. Do not infer likelihood from the shading or select a policy solely because one cell is smaller.

For a real review, compare coverage definitions and limits, the applicable deductible structure, accessible reserves, the premium schedule and the household’s tolerance for a large cash call. Obtain the actual policy terms and resolve coverage questions with the insurer or licensed representative. The graphs organize the funding trade-off while leaving underwriting and suitability outside the calculator.
